knowledge: Neurodevelopmental disorder with or without variable brain abnormalities (NEDBEBA; OMIM #618443) is caused by heterozygous de novo (or rarely inherited) variants in MAPK8IP3 (mitogen-activated protein kinase 8 interacting protein 3, encoding JIP3). Major initial descriptions appeared in 2019 (e.g., Platzer et al., PMID: 31130283; Iwasawa et al., PMID: 31130282). Phenotypically, affected individuals present with intellectual disability/global developmental delay, profound speech impairment/lack of speech, variable tone abnormalities (axial hypotonia often progressing to or co-occurring with appendicular spasticity/hypertonia), and distinct structural brain anomalies on MRI including hypoplasia or agenesis of the corpus callosum, cerebellar vermis or hemisphere hypoplasia, progressive cerebral atrophy, and periventricular white matter volume loss. Peripheral/sensorimotor axonal neuropathy or spastic paraplegia phenotypes have also been described in subsets, particularly correlating with specific variant locations or inheritance patterns.
prior_hypothesis: A clinical presentation dominated by global developmental delay/severe intellectual disability, early-onset axial hypotonia with lower-limb spasticity, non-specific mild facial dysmorphism, optic atrophy/cortical visual impairment, and specific brain MRI abnormalities (prominently thin or absent corpus callosum and cerebellar atrophy/hypoplasia) strongly points toward MAPK8IP3-related neurodevelopmental disorder. While no single feature is 100% pathognomonic in isolation, the constellation of spastic quadriparesis/diplegia with early cerebellar and callosal anomalies, without prominent metabolic decompensations or visceral storage, strongly distinguishes it from mimickers like cerebral palsy or hereditary spastic paraplegias.

candidate_answers.answer: Developmental delay / Intellectual disability is present in nearly 100% of reported patients (e.g., Platzer et al. 2019 reported 13/13, HP:0001249/HP:0001263; Iwasawa et al. 2019 reported 8/8), usually moderate-to-profound with severe expressive language deficit.

Structural neuroimaging abnormalities occur in >85% of cases; specifically, corpus callosum hypoplasia/dysgenesis (approx. 9/13 in Platzer et al., HP:0002079) and cerebellar vermis/hemispheric hypoplasia or atrophy (approx. 8/13 in Platzer et al., HP:0001321) serve as key imaging markers.

Tone abnormalities, specifically early infantile hypotonia (HP:0001252) followed by or combined with progressive spasticity or hyperreflexia (HP:0001257), appear in >70-80% of individuals across major cohorts.

The primary differential diagnoses include hereditary spastic paraplegias (e.g., SPG11, SPG15), Pelizaeus-Merzbacher-like disorders, and classic cerebral palsy; MAPK8IP3 is distinguished from simple CP by progressive/evolutionary MRI findings (cerebellar/cerebral volume loss) and genetic etiology, and from pure HSP by severe early intellectual disability and microcephaly.

Genotype-phenotype correlations show that recurrent de novo missense variants clustering in conserved leucine zipper and JNK-binding domains tend to produce severe syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotypes with structural brain defects, whereas some distal truncating or specific missense variants may associate with isolated spastic paraplegia or lower motor neuron involvement without profound brain malformations.

open_questions: What are the precise exact cohort numerators and denominators for secondary features such as seizures/epilepsy, cortical visual impairment, and microcephaly across all published series?
Are there recurrent missense hotspots (such as p.Arg260 or specific coiled-coil domain residues) that strictly correlate with cerebellar hypoplasia versus normal imaging?
What specific non-neurological organ manifestations (cardiac, renal, skeletal), if any, have been consistently ruled absent across systematically evaluated cohorts?
assumptions: Assumed that OMIM #618443 primarily encompasses both dominant de novo missense/in-frame variant cohorts (Platzer 2019, Iwasawa 2019) and any subsequent expansions to the phenotypic spectrum.
Assumed that the primary clinical confusion occurs with static encephalopathy (cerebral palsy) and complex forms of hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) or pontocerebellar hypoplasia.
